summary: Specifies IANA parameter assignment considerations for DNS, covering resource record types, classes, opcodes, error codes, header bits and AFSDB subtypes. It obsoletes RFC 6195 and updates RFC 1183, RFC 2845, RFC 2930 and RFC 3597. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: The rulebook for how new items get added to the official lists of DNS words, codes and labels.

subtitle: The rulebook for who may add new record types, classes, opcodes and error codes to the DNS registries.

tldr.problem: DNS has many numbered fields (record types, classes, opcodes, error codes, header bits), and without clear rules for handing out new values, two parties could claim the same number or break existing software.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets an allocation policy for each range of each registry, such as Standards Action, IETF Review or Expert Review, and describes a template and a two-week expert review for new record types.
tldr.outcome: It replaced RFC 6195 with a faster RRTYPE process and closed the AFSDB subtype registry.

facts.label: Extended RCODE size
facts.value: 12 bits (4 header bits plus 8 from OPT)

today: RFC 6895 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 42) that obsoleted RFC 6195. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What This RFC Governs
sections.content:
RFC 6895 gives the general IANA parameter assignment rules for the Domain Name System. It covers DNS resource record types, CLASSes, operation codes (OpCodes), error codes (RCODEs), DNS message header bits and AFSDB resource record subtypes. It is a Best Current Practice and assumes the reader already knows the core DNS specifications, RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, among others.

It obsoletes RFC 6195. The RFC says the only significant changes are to the RRTYPE allocation process, which was streamlined, and the closing of the AFSDB subtype registry. It also updates RFC 1183, RFC 2845, RFC 2930 and RFC 3597. The policy names (Standards Action, IETF Review, Specification Required, Private Use) are used as defined in RFC 5226.
sections.eli5: It is the rulebook for adding new entries to the official lists that DNS uses, like a library deciding who may add a new book code.

sections.title: Header Bits and OpCodes
sections.content:
The DNS header has an ID, a row of flag bits (QR, AA, TC, RD, RA, Z, AD, CD), a 4-bit OpCode, a 4-bit RCODE and four count fields. The QR bit says whether a message is a query or a response. The AA, TC, RD, RA and CD bits each make sense only in queries or only in responses. Only RD and CD are expected to be copied from query to response, but some implementations copy the whole query header. Giving a bit a new meaning is therefore dangerous, and meanings for these bits may only be assigned by a Standards Action.

The Z bit is the spare one. Some ancient implementations used it in queries to mean that only the zone's primary server's answer was acceptable. Current implementations are believed to ignore it, and giving it a meaning also requires a Standards Action.

Assigned OpCodes are 0 Query, 1 IQuery (obsolete), 2 Status, 4 Notify and 5 Update. Value 3 and values 6 to 15 are unassigned. New OpCodes need a Standards Action, with early allocation permitted as specified in RFC 4020.
sections.eli5: The header is the front of an envelope with little checkboxes. Changing what a checkbox means could confuse every mailroom, so only the strictest approval process may do it.

sections.title: Error Codes (RCODEs)
sections.content:
The header has room for only four bits of RCODE, but error codes also appear in TSIG records, TKEY records and, through the OPT record, in a 12-bit extended field. The OPT RR adds 8 bits to the 4 header bits. The TSIG and TKEY records have a 16-bit Error field.

RFC 6895 declares one unified error number space for all of these places, which is why it updates RFC 2845 and RFC 2930. Except for 9 and 16, the same number must not be assigned to different errors, even if they would only occur in different record types. The duplicate use of 16 (BADVERS in the OPT RR, BADSIG in TSIG) was accidental.

Error 9 (NotAuth) has two meanings. In a response without a TSIG RR, or with a TSIG RR whose error field is zero, it means Not Authoritative. In a response with a TSIG RR that has a non-zero error field, it means Not Authorized.

Values 11 to 15 and 23 to 3,840 are unassigned, 3,841 to 4,095 are reserved for Private Use, and 65,535 can only be allocated by Standards Action. A new RCODE in an unassigned range requires an IETF Review.
sections.eli5: Error codes are like numbered excuse cards. All the places that use excuse cards now share one deck, so no two different excuses carry the same number (with two exceptions).

sections.title: Resource Record Types and Classes
sections.content:
Every resource record has a NAME, a 2-octet TYPE, a 2-octet CLASS, a 4-octet TTL, a 16-bit RDLENGTH and variable-length RDATA. A TTL of zero means the record can only be used for the transaction in progress.

RRTYPEs fall into three groups: data TYPEs, which store data; QTYPEs, which appear only in queries; and Meta-TYPEs, which describe transient data tied to one message. The Meta-TYPEs are OPT, TSIG and TKEY, and the QTYPEs are the wildcard type (ALL/ANY), MAILA, MAILB, AXFR and IXFR. Mnemonics must start with a capital letter, use only capital letters, digits and hyphens, and end with a letter or digit. They must not look like the generic TYPEnnn or CLASSnnn names from RFC 3597, and must not clash with CLASS names. RRTYPE 0 must never be allocated for ordinary use, 1 to 127 are for data TYPEs, 128 to 255 for Q and Meta-TYPEs, and 256 to 61,439 for data RRTYPEs. The range 65,280 to 65,534 is Private Use.

CLASSes work similarly. IN is 1, Chaos (CH) is 3 and Hesiod (HS) is 4. Class 2 is available by IETF Review, as are 5 to 127 (data CLASSes only) and 256 to 32,767. The ranges 32,768 to 57,343 and 57,344 to 65,279 use Specification Required. The RFC notes that the IN class has dominated DNS use.
sections.eli5: Each record in DNS has a type tag and a family tag. There are reserved number blocks for each kind of tag, plus a block anyone can use privately for experiments.

sections.title: How a New RRTYPE Gets Allocated
sections.content:
New RRTYPE values in the open ranges are allocated by Expert Review under the DNS RRTYPE Allocation Policy, provided two requirements are met. First, a complete template (Appendix A) has been posted to the dns-rrtype-applications@ietf.org mailing list and received by the Expert. Second, the RR is either a data TYPE that can be handled as an Unknown RR under RFC 3597, or a Meta-TYPE whose processing is optional, so it is safe to discard. Requests that do not meet these can still be allocated by Standards Action.

The IESG appoints a small pool of Experts, and IANA picks one for each application. The Expert has no more than two weeks to approve or reject, informing IANA, the applicant and the dnsext list. No answer in that time counts as rejection. IANA keeps a public archive of approved templates.

Experts should normally be lenient and prefer to approve. They should usually reject a request that is unclear or incomplete, that affects DNS processing without meeting requirement two, that makes wrong assumptions about wildcards, CNAME or DNAME, or that asks for an excessive number of values when a smaller number or Private Use values would do.

The Appendix A template asks for submission type, kind of RR, contact details, motivation, a description, the closest existing RRTYPEs and why they fall short, an optional mnemonic, any registry needs, and whether servers or resolvers would need changes that stop the type from being handled as unknown.
sections.eli5: To get a new type code, you fill in a form and send it to a volunteer expert. The expert should say yes unless the form is unclear or risky, and must answer within two weeks.

sections.title: Labels, OPT and AFSDB
sections.content:
DNS names are sequences of labels. There are data labels and compression labels, which are pointers that shorten the wire encoding of names. The two data label types are Text and Binary. Text labels are matched without regard to ASCII case, and the Binary label type is Historic. The last label of every NAME is the zero-length ROOT label, which cannot be used for any other purpose. NAMEs are local to a CLASS, and the RFC calls IN the only DNS class in global use on the Internet at the time.

The OPT RR (RRTYPE 41) is specified in RFC 6891. It extends the effective size of several fields, including RCODE from 4 to 12 bits.

The AFSDB RR has the same RDATA structure as the MX RR, with a 16-bit subtype first. Using AFSDB to locate AFS cell database servers was deprecated by RFC 5864. RFC 6895 closes the subtype registry, so no new subtypes can be allocated. Only 1 (AFS v3.0 Location Service) and 2 (DCE/NCA root cell directory node) are assigned.
sections.eli5: A name is a chain of labels ending in an empty one called the root. The old list of AFSDB sub-kinds is now locked, like a sign saying no more entries.

sections.title: Security and IANA Duties
sections.content:
The security section is short: the document addresses IANA considerations for general DNS parameters, not security, and points to RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035 for secure DNS.

The IANA section says the document consists entirely of DNS IANA considerations. IANA has set up a process for accepting templates and choosing an Expert, forwards each template to the Expert with a copy to the applicant, and archives approved templates and referenced documents. The applicant must post the formal template to the dns-rrtype-applications list, which IANA monitors.
sections.eli5: This rulebook is about handing out numbers, not about keeping secrets. For secrets and safety, it sends you to the DNS security documents.

fields.name: ID
fields.desc: Identifies the query and is echoed in the response.

fields.name: RD
fields.desc: Flag bit, expected to be copied to the response.

fields.name: Z
fields.desc: The spare bit; a meaning needs a Standards Action.

fields.name: CD
fields.desc: Flag bit, expected to be copied to the response.

fields.name: QDCOUNT/ZOCOUNT
fields.desc: Records in the question (or zone) section.

fields.name: ANCOUNT/PRCOUNT
fields.desc: Records in the answer (or prerequisite) section.

fields.name: NSCOUNT/UPCOUNT
fields.desc: Records in the authority (or update) section.

fields.name: ARCOUNT
fields.desc: Records in the additional information section.

items.label: Status
items.desc: Reserved in RFC 1035; behavior not specified.

items.label: Unassigned
items.desc: New values need a Standards Action.

items.label: NotAuth
items.desc: Not Authoritative, or Not Authorized when a TSIG RR has a non-zero error field.

items.label: BADVERS / BADSIG
items.desc: Bad OPT Version in OPT; TSIG Signature Failure in TSIG.
